title: Google Gemini ADK: Build Agents That Ship
description: Learn Google's Agent Development Kit from your first local agent to production deployment. AI Studio keys, function tools, workflow agents, multi-agent teams, MCP and A2A protocols, trajectory evaluation, and deploying to Agent Runtime and Cloud Run.

lessons.title: The Agent Framework Landscape
lessons.bodyMd:
## From Chatbots to Agents

A chatbot answers questions. An agent does work. That distinction sounds small, but it changes everything about how you build.

A chatbot takes one input, produces one output, and forgets you exist. An agent keeps going: it plans, calls tools, reads the results, adjusts, and only stops when the job is done or it genuinely needs your help. Ordering supplies, triaging support tickets, reconciling invoices, these are jobs with steps, branches, and judgment calls. That is agent territory.

The last few years produced a crowded field of frameworks for building these systems. LangChain showed developers that chaining model calls with tools was powerful. CrewAI made multi-agent role-play teams fashionable. AutoGPT proved that fully autonomous loops were exciting but hard to trust. OpenAI's Assistants API and function calling made tool use mainstream. Each one taught the industry something, and each one left gaps: brittle orchestration, no standard way to evaluate whether an agent did the right thing, and a painful cliff between a local demo and something you could deploy.

## Where ADK Comes In

Google's Agent Development Kit, usually called ADK, is Google's open-source answer to those gaps. It is a code-first framework for building, debugging, and deploying AI agents, and it was designed with one belief: the same code you prototype locally should be able to run in production at enterprise scale without a rewrite.

ADK is optimized for Gemini models but it is not locked to Google's cloud. You can develop agents on your laptop using a free API key from Google AI Studio, run them in the built-in `adk web` development UI, and later deploy the same agent to Google's Agent Runtime, Cloud Run, or a Kubernetes cluster. That local-to-production path is the whole pitch: prototype fast, harden deliberately, deploy the same artifact.

## What "Enterprise Scale" Actually Means Here

The word enterprise gets thrown around a lot. In ADK's case it points at four concrete capabilities. First, flexible orchestration: you can define predictable pipelines with workflow agents, or let agents route dynamically when the task needs adaptability. Second, native multi-agent support: you compose teams of specialized agents that delegate to each other, rather than stuffing every capability into one giant prompt. Third, a real tool ecosystem: pre-built integrations plus your own Python, TypeScript, Go, or Java code. Fourth, built-in evaluation: tools that test execution trajectories, so you can measure whether your agent behaves correctly instead of eyeballing chat transcripts.

## The Mental Model

Think of ADK as three layers. At the bottom, agents: the units that reason, each with an instruction, a model, and a set of tools. In the middle, orchestration: how agents hand work to each other, in fixed sequences or dynamic teams. At the top, the runtime: where agents execute, with sessions, state, and deployment targets.

If you have built automations in n8n or Make, you already understand the pipeline half of this. If you have written prompts for Claude Code or ChatGPT, you understand the reasoning half. ADK is what happens when you fuse those two instincts into one framework: deterministic where you need control, agentic where you need judgment.

## What You Will Build in This Guide

By the end you will have built a working agent locally, given it custom tools, composed it into a multi-agent team, evaluated its behavior, and understood exactly what deploying it to production involves. No Google Cloud billing account required for the first four chapters. A free AI Studio key is enough.

lessons.title: ADK vs LangChain vs CrewAI: An Honest Comparison
lessons.bodyMd:
## Why Compare at All

Choosing a framework is a real decision with real costs. Migrating agents later is painful, so it pays to understand the trade-offs up front. This lesson compares ADK against the two frameworks you are most likely to encounter: LangChain and CrewAI.

## LangChain: The Pioneer

LangChain was the first framework to make "model plus tools plus memory" feel like a coherent programming model. Its strengths are maturity and ecosystem: thousands of integrations, deep documentation, and LangSmith for observability. If your team already runs LangChain in production, switching is rarely worth it.

The honest weaknesses: LangChain grew fast and accumulated complexity. Its abstractions (chains, agents, runnables) can feel like a framework you have to learn instead of a tool that gets out of your way. Debugging a failing LangChain agent often means spelunking through nested callbacks. ADK's response is simplicity: an agent is a small, explicit object with an instruction, a model, and tools. The framework does less magic, which means fewer surprises.

## CrewAI: The Team Builder

CrewAI made multi-agent systems accessible with an appealing metaphor: define agents with roles, give them tasks, and let them collaborate like a crew. It is genuinely good for role-based decompositions like researcher plus writer plus editor.

The honest weaknesses: the crew metaphor can become a straitjacket. When your workflow needs a strict sequence with validation gates, or when you need fine-grained control over state, the role-play abstraction fights you. ADK's workflow agents (sequential, parallel, loop) give you the deterministic pipeline option directly, and its multi-agent delegation gives you the team option without forcing everything through the crew metaphor.

## ADK's Distinct Bets

ADK makes four bets its competitors do not fully share. First, the dev UI: `adk web` gives you a local playground with event tracing, session inspection, and state viewing out of the box. LangChain needs LangSmith for comparable visibility, and that is a separate service. Second, evaluation as a first-class citizen: ADK ships trajectory evaluation, so you can assert on what the agent did, not just what it said. Third, deployment continuity: the same agent code runs locally, on Cloud Run, or on Agent Runtime. Fourth, Google's native integrations: Search grounding, BigQuery, and the wider Google Cloud data stack are first-class tools, which matters enormously if your data already lives in BigQuery.

## The Fair Caveats

ADK is younger than LangChain, so its third-party integration catalog is smaller. If you need an obscure SaaS connector today, LangChain probably has it and ADK probably does not, though ADK's MCP support closes this gap quickly. ADK is also most at home in the Google ecosystem; if your stack is AWS-native with Bedrock models, the fit is weaker. And while ADK supports multiple languages, Python is where the docs, samples, and community momentum concentrate.

## The Decision Rule

Pick ADK when: you want local prototyping that graduates to Google Cloud deployment, you care about evaluating agent behavior rigorously, you want explicit control over orchestration, or your data lives in Google's stack. Pick LangChain when: you need maximum integration breadth or your team already knows it. Pick CrewAI when: your problem decomposes cleanly into roles and you want the fastest path to a demo. None of these choices is permanent, and the concepts transfer.

lessons.title: When Google's Stack Fits (and When It Doesn't)
lessons.bodyMd:
## The Two Doors Into ADK

Google gives you two ways to build agents, and beginners often confuse them. Door one is Google AI Studio: a free, browser-based playground where you get a Gemini API key, test prompts, tune parameters, and export code. It is perfect for learning and prototyping. Door two is Vertex AI and the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: the production path with IAM, VPC controls, model garden access, and Agent Runtime deployment.

ADK spans both doors. You develop with an AI Studio key on your laptop, and when the agent is ready, you point the same code at Vertex AI credentials and deploy. Understanding this two-door model saves you from the most common beginner mistake: assuming you need a Cloud billing account and a project to start. You do not. Start in AI Studio.

## When the Fit Is Great

ADK shines brightest in four situations. First, data gravity: if your organization's data lives in BigQuery, Google Drive, or other Google services, ADK's native integrations turn painful plumbing into configuration. Second, search-grounded agents: the built-in Google Search tool gives agents fresh, cited information with far less hallucination risk than a bare model. Third, regulated or audited workflows: the combination of deterministic workflow agents and trajectory evaluation gives compliance-minded teams the control and evidence they crave. Fourth, multi-agent systems that need to grow: start with one agent, add specialists, add workflow gates, deploy, all in one framework.

## When to Look Elsewhere

Be honest about the mismatches too. If you need a fully no-code builder for non-technical teammates, ADK is the wrong tool; it is code-first by design, and platforms with visual builders serve that audience better. If your agents must run entirely on-device or in air-gapped environments, a cloud-model framework is a non-starter. If your company has standardized on another cloud's agent stack, the integration tax of crossing clouds usually outweighs ADK's benefits. And if you just need a thin wrapper around one model call, you do not need an agent framework at all; the Gemini API directly is simpler.

## The Cost Question

Beginners worry about cost, so here is the practical picture. AI Studio's free tier lets you build and test agents at zero cost within generous rate limits, which is plenty for learning and prototypes. When you move to Vertex AI for production, you pay standard Gemini model pricing per token plus the compute for wherever the agent runs. ADK itself is open source and free. The expensive mistakes are architectural, not licensing: an agent that loops 40 times calling a Pro-class model on every turn will cost more than a well-designed workflow that uses a Flash-class model for routing and reserves the big model for hard reasoning. Chapter 5 covers cost monitoring in detail.

## Your Path Through This Guide

Chapters 2 and 3 need nothing but a free AI Studio key and Python on your laptop. Chapter 4 stays local too. Only Chapter 5 touches production deployment, and even there you will learn the concepts and commands without being forced to spend money. By the end you will know exactly where ADK fits in your toolkit, and you will have the muscle memory to reach for it when the fit is right.

lessons.title: Your Gemini API Key from AI Studio
lessons.bodyMd:
## What AI Studio Is

Google AI Studio, at aistudio.google.com, is Google's free developer playground for Gemini. Think of it as the workbench where every Gemini project starts: you sign in with a Google account, generate an API key, test prompts against real models, tune parameters like temperature, try structured output, and export working code. For ADK development, AI Studio is your key provider and your prompt laboratory.

## Getting Your Key

The flow takes about two minutes. Sign in to AI Studio with a Google account. Open the API key section and create a new key. Copy it immediately into a safe place. That key authenticates your ADK agents to the Gemini API, and it is free within the published rate limits, which are generous enough for all the building in this guide.

Treat this key like a password. Never paste it into chat windows, never commit it to git, and never hardcode it into your agent files. You will store it in a `.env` file that your project ignores via `.gitignore`. If a key ever leaks, delete it in AI Studio and generate a fresh one; rotation takes seconds.

## The Prompt Playground

Before you write any agent code, spend fifteen minutes in the AI Studio prompt area. This is where you develop the instincts that make your agents good, because an ADK agent's behavior comes mostly from its instruction text, and the playground is the fastest place to iterate on instructions.

Try this exercise: pick a Gemini Flash model, write a system instruction like "You are a meeting scheduler. Always confirm the timezone before proposing times. Never invent attendee availability.", then test it with tricky inputs. Watch how temperature changes the tone. Lower values make the agent consistent and careful; higher values make it creative and unpredictable. For agents, you usually want low temperature on the routing and extraction steps and moderate temperature on the drafting steps. Learning this feel in the playground saves hours of debugging later.

## Structured Output and the Prompt Gallery

Two AI Studio features deserve special attention. Structured output lets you constrain the model to return valid JSON matching a schema you define, which is how you get reliable data out of an agent instead of prose you have to parse. The prompt gallery is a library of pre-built prompts demonstrating long context, multimodality, structured output, and tool use. Browse it the way a chef browses recipes: not to copy, but to learn techniques.

## Model Selection Basics

AI Studio lets you switch between Gemini models, and this choice follows your agents into ADK. The Flash family is fast and cheap, ideal for routing, classification, and high-volume steps. The Pro family reasons harder and costs more, ideal for the difficult judgment calls. A common production pattern is routing with Flash and escalating to Pro only when the task demands it. In this guide we will mostly use a Flash-class model so your free-tier key goes far, and Chapter 5 shows how to mix models deliberately.

lessons.title: Installing ADK and Creating Your First Agent
lessons.bodyMd:
## Prerequisites

You need Python 3.9 or newer and `pip`. That is the whole list for local development. ADK also ships in TypeScript, Go, and Java, but this guide uses Python throughout because that is where the documentation, samples, and community examples are richest. Everything you learn transfers to the other languages.

## Installation

Create a project folder, set up a virtual environment, and install the package:

```bash
mkdir adk-first-agent && cd adk-first-agent
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install google-adk
```

One command, one package. Verify it worked:

```bash
adk --help
```

You should see the ADK command-line interface with subcommands like `run`, `web`, `create`, and `eval`. If the command is not found, your virtual environment is not activated.

## The Agent Package Layout

ADK discovers agents as Python packages, which is just a folder with a specific shape. For an agent called `greeter`, create this structure:

```
adk-first-agent/
  greeter/
    __init__.py
    agent.py
    .env
```

The `__init__.py` file is one line:

```python
from . import agent
```

The `.env` file holds your key, and nothing else needs to live there yet:

```
GOOGLE_API_KEY=your_key_here
```

Add `.env` to your `.gitignore` right now, before you forget. Every ADK tutorial repeats this because every ADK beginner eventually commits a key.

## Your First Agent

Now the actual agent, in `greeter/agent.py`:

```python
from google.adk.agents import Agent

root_agent = Agent(
    name="greeter",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="A friendly greeter that welcomes users warmly.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a warm, concise greeter. Welcome the user, "
        "ask their name if you do not know it, and offer one "
        "helpful suggestion for what to try next."
    ),
)
```

Four fields do almost all the work. The `name` identifies the agent. The `model` picks which Gemini model reasons for it. The `description` is a short summary other agents use when deciding whether to delegate to this one. The `instruction` is the system prompt: the agent's job description, personality, and rules. ADK looks for a module-level variable literally named `root_agent`; that is the entry point the CLI and dev UI will load.

## Running It

From the folder containing `greeter`, run:

```bash
adk run greeter
```

You get an interactive chat session in your terminal. Try it, then type `exit` to quit. Congratulations: you have a running agent. It does not do much yet, which is exactly the point. The next lessons give it tools, memory, and teammates.

## The `adk create` Shortcut

If you prefer scaffolding, `adk create` generates this folder structure for you interactively, asking which model backend to use. It is handy, but building the files by hand once teaches you the layout permanently. You now know what every file does, which pays off the moment something breaks.

lessons.title: The adk web Dev UI Tour
lessons.bodyMd:
## Why a Dev UI Matters

Most agent frameworks make you debug by staring at terminal logs. ADK ships a local web application, launched with `adk web`, that gives you a visual debugger for your agents: chat with them, inspect the event stream, view session state, and trace exactly which tools ran with which arguments. Learning this UI early will save you more time than any other single habit in this guide.

## Launching It

From the directory that contains your agent folders, run:

```bash
adk web
```

Open the printed localhost address in your browser. The UI discovers every agent package under your current directory and lists them in a picker. This is why the folder layout from the last lesson matters: `adk web` finds agents by scanning for packages containing a `root_agent`.

## The Four Panes

The interface centers on four areas. The chat pane is where you talk to the selected agent, just like the CLI but with richer rendering. The events pane is the gold mine: every model call, tool invocation, and state change appears as a structured event with timing and payloads. When an agent misbehaves, this is where you find out whether the model reasoned badly, called the wrong tool, or passed bad arguments. The session pane shows the conversation history and metadata for the current session. The state pane shows the agent's key-value state, which becomes important once your agents start remembering things across turns.

## Debugging With Events

Here is the debugging loop you will use constantly. Reproduce the bad behavior in chat. Open the events pane and find the turn where things went wrong. Read the model's reasoning and the exact tool call it made. Nine times out of ten, the fix is obvious at this point: the instruction was ambiguous, a tool description misled the model, or the arguments were malformed. Fix the instruction or the tool, rerun, and confirm the event stream looks right. This loop is dramatically faster than adding print statements and rerunning blind.

## Sessions Are Cheap: Use Them

Each conversation in the dev UI is a session with its own state and history. Start fresh sessions liberally when testing; stale history is a notorious source of "it worked a minute ago" confusion. The UI lets you create new sessions in one click. Get in the habit of testing each behavior change in a fresh session so you know the improvement came from your change, not from leftover context.

## Dev UI vs Production

One honest limitation: `adk web` is a development tool, not a deployment target. It runs on your machine, with your key, for an audience of one developer. Real users get the deployed agent from Chapter 5. The dev UI's job is to make the agent correct before it ever meets a user, and it is excellent at that job.

lessons.title: First Agent in 10 Minutes: A Time and Weather Helper
lessons.bodyMd:
## The Plan

You will build an agent that tells the current time and fetches a weather summary. This exercises the two most important ADK skills: defining function tools and watching the model decide when to call them. Set a timer; this genuinely takes about ten minutes.

## Step 1: The Tool Functions

Tools in ADK can be plain Python functions. The model's view of your tool comes from the function name, its docstring, and its type hints, so write all three carefully. Create a new agent folder called `helper` with the standard `__init__.py` and `.env`, then write `helper/agent.py`:

```python
from google.adk.agents import Agent
from datetime import datetime
import zoneinfo


def get_current_time(timezone: str) -> dict:
    '''Get the current time in a given IANA timezone.

    Args:
        timezone: IANA timezone name, e.g. "America/Chicago".

    Returns:
        Dictionary with the timezone and the current local time.
    '''
    try:
        tz = zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(timezone)
    except Exception:
        return {"error": f"Unknown timezone: {timezone}"}
    now = datetime.now(tz)
    return {"timezone": timezone, "time": now.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")}


def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    '''Get a weather summary for a city.

    Args:
        city: City name, e.g. "Chicago".

    Returns:
        Dictionary with a short weather summary.
    '''
    summaries = {
        "chicago": "62F and windy, with a chance of dramatic lake-effect mood swings.",
        "austin": "88F and sunny. Hydrate.",
    }
    return {"city": city, "summary": summaries.get(city.lower(), "Weather data unavailable for this city.")}
```

The weather tool is intentionally a stub with two cities. In a real agent you would call a weather API here; the stub keeps this lesson focused on ADK mechanics rather than API keys for third-party services.

## Step 2: Wire the Tools to the Agent

```python
root_agent = Agent(
    name="helper",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Answers time and weather questions.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a helpful assistant. Use get_current_time when the user "
        "asks about the time, always confirming the timezone first if it is "
        "ambiguous. Use get_weather for weather questions. If you do not "
        "know a city, say so instead of guessing."
    ),
    tools=[get_current_time, get_weather],
)
```

Notice the instruction does real work: it tells the model when to use each tool and, critically, what to do when information is missing. "Say so instead of guessing" is the kind of line that prevents entire categories of bad behavior.

## Step 3: Run and Interrogate

Launch `adk web`, select the helper agent, and try: "What time is it in Chicago?" Watch the events pane. You should see the model call `get_current_time` with `timezone="America/Chicago"`, receive the result, and answer. Then try "What is the weather like in Paris?" and confirm it says the data is unavailable rather than inventing weather. Then try the adversarial one: "What time is it?" with no location, and confirm it asks for the timezone instead of assuming.

## What You Just Learned

In ten minutes you covered the ADK core loop: define tools as documented functions, describe the agent's job in the instruction, and let the model orchestrate. Everything from here on is elaboration: more tools, memory across turns, multiple agents, and deployment. The shape never changes.

lessons.title: Agents: Instruction, Model, and Tools
lessons.bodyMd:
## The Agent Is a Small Object

An ADK agent is deliberately simple: a name, a model, an instruction, a description, and a list of tools. There is no hidden machinery to memorize. This simplicity is a design choice. When agent behavior goes wrong, and it will, you want exactly three places to look: the instruction, the tools, or the model choice. Small objects make for short debugging sessions.

```python
from google.adk.agents import Agent

root_agent = Agent(
    name="support_triage",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Classifies incoming support tickets and routes them.",
    instruction=(
        "You triage support tickets. Read each ticket, classify it as "
        "billing, technical, or account, and explain your reasoning in one "
        "sentence. Never promise refunds; only the billing team can do that."
    ),
    tools=[lookup_order, search_knowledge_base],
)
```

## Writing Instructions That Work

The instruction is the highest-leverage text you will write. Good instructions share four traits. They state the role in one sentence. They define the scope: what the agent handles and what it must escalate. They give decision rules for the ambiguous cases you have actually seen, not hypothetical ones. And they specify output shape: what the answer should look like.

Write instructions from real failures. Every time your agent mishandles something in the dev UI, add one sentence to the instruction that would have prevented it. Over weeks, this builds an instruction that encodes your operational knowledge. Resist the urge to write a thirty-line instruction on day one; start short and let reality edit it.

## The Description Field Matters More Than You Think

The `description` is not documentation for humans. It is how other agents decide whether to delegate work to this agent. In a multi-agent team, a coordinator reads each specialist's description and routes tasks accordingly. A vague description like "handles stuff" produces vague routing. A crisp one like "Classifies support tickets into billing, technical, or account categories" produces correct routing. Write descriptions as if a busy manager is skimming them, because that is effectively what is happening.

## Choosing the Model

The `model` parameter names the Gemini model that does the reasoning. Flash-class models are fast and economical: use them for classification, routing, extraction, and any high-volume step where the reasoning is straightforward. Pro-class models reason harder: use them for ambiguous judgment calls, complex planning, and anything where a mistake is expensive. You can mix models within one system, which Chapter 5 covers as a cost strategy. When in doubt, start with Flash; upgrade the specific agents that prove too dumb in evaluation, rather than paying Pro prices everywhere preemptively.

lessons.title: Tools: Function Tools and Built-in Power
lessons.bodyMd:
## Tools Are How Agents Touch the World

A model without tools can only talk. A model with tools can act: query databases, call APIs, search the web, run code. In ADK, the most common tool is a plain Python function with a clear name, a docstring, and type hints. The framework converts it into a tool definition the model can understand, executes it when the model calls it, and returns the result into the conversation.

## The Anatomy of a Good Function Tool

Three things determine whether the model uses your tool correctly. The function name should be a verb phrase describing the action: `lookup_order`, not `order_stuff`. The docstring should describe when to use the tool and what each argument means, because the model reads the docstring as the tool's manual. The type hints should be precise, because they become the tool's parameter schema. Return dictionaries, not prose, so the model gets structured data it can reason over reliably.

```python
def lookup_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    '''Look up an order by its ID.

    Args:
        order_id: The order ID, e.g. "ORD-1234".

    Returns:
        Dictionary with order status, items, and total. Includes an
        "error" key if the order is not found.
    '''
    order = ORDERS_DB.get(order_id)
    if order is None:
        return {"error": f"Order {order_id} not found."}
    return {"order_id": order_id, **order}
```

Error returns deserve the same care as success returns. A tool that raises an unhandled exception gives the model a confusing stack trace; a tool that returns `{"error": "..."}` gives the model something it can explain to the user and recover from.

## Built-in Tools

ADK ships pre-built tools so you do not reinvent common capabilities. The headline one is Google Search grounding: give your agent the search tool and it can answer questions about current events, verify facts, and cite sources, dramatically reducing hallucinations on anything time-sensitive. There are also tools for code execution and integrations with Google services. Prefer a built-in tool over a hand-rolled one whenever it fits; maintained code beats your weekend code.

## Tool Design Discipline

Keep tools narrow. One tool should do one thing well. A `manage_customer` tool that looks up, updates, and deletes is three tools wearing a trench coat, and the model will confuse the operations. Keep tools side-effect-aware: mark which tools read and which tools write, and give the agent explicit instruction about when writing is allowed. The scariest agent failures come from write tools with vague instructions. Finally, keep tools fast or make them async; a tool that blocks for thirty seconds makes the whole agent feel broken even when it is working correctly.

lessons.title: Sessions and State
lessons.bodyMd:
## Why Agents Need Memory

A single chat turn is stateless: the model sees the conversation and responds. Real work spans turns. A support agent needs to remember the order ID from three messages ago. A research agent needs to accumulate findings. ADK handles this with two mechanisms: sessions, which scope a conversation, and state, which stores key-value data the agent can read and write across turns.

## Sessions in Practice

Every conversation with an agent happens inside a session. In the dev UI, each chat thread is a session; starting a new chat starts a new session with empty state and history. Programmatically, you work with a session service that creates sessions, appends events, and retrieves history. The practical rule is simple: one session per user task. Do not reuse sessions across unrelated tasks, because leftover context bleeds into new work and produces the classic "it worked until it suddenly didn't" mystery.

## State: The Agent's Notebook

State is a dictionary the agent can update as it works. A triage agent might store `state["ticket_category"] = "billing"` after classifying, so later steps can branch on it without re-reading the ticket. Tools can read and write state too, which is how a database lookup tool can stash results for the next step.

```python
def save_summary(summary: str, state) -> dict:
    '''Save the research summary to session state.'''
    state["summary"] = summary
    return {"saved": True}
```

State persists for the life of the session and, depending on your session service configuration, can persist across sessions for the same user. That persistence is powerful and dangerous in equal measure: it enables "remember my preferences" features, and it enables stale-data bugs. Name state keys explicitly, document what writes them, and expire anything time-sensitive.

A useful convention is namespacing your keys by the step that owns them, like `triage_category` instead of just `category`. When two agents write to the same flat namespace, collisions produce bugs that look like the model is confused when the real problem is two writers overwriting each other. A few extra characters in the key name buys you hours of debugging you will never have to do.

## What the Model Sees

Here is the part beginners miss: the model does not automatically see everything in state. ADK controls which state is injected into the model's context. This is a feature, not a limitation. Dumping an entire session's accumulated data into every prompt wastes tokens and distracts the model. Instead, design which facts each step needs and let the framework assemble focused context. When an agent seems to "forget" something you stored, the bug is almost always in what gets injected, not in the storage itself. Check the events pane in the dev UI: it shows exactly what context each model call received.

lessons.title: Workflow Agents: Sequential, Parallel, and Loop
lessons.bodyMd:
## Determinism Where It Counts

Not every step needs an LLM's judgment. Fetching an order, then checking inventory, then drafting an email is a pipeline: the order of operations is known, and each step's inputs come from the previous step's outputs. ADK's workflow agents express these pipelines explicitly, which makes them testable, cheap, and auditable. Use workflow agents for the predictable skeleton of your system and reserve agentic reasoning for the steps that genuinely need it.

## SequentialAgent: The Assembly Line

A sequential agent runs sub-agents in order, passing results downstream. Think of a content pipeline: researcher gathers facts, writer drafts, editor polishes. Each step is itself an agent with its own instruction and tools, but the orchestration is fixed.

```python
from google.adk.agents import Agent, SequentialAgent

researcher = Agent(
    name="researcher",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Gathers facts on a topic.",
    instruction="Research the given topic using search. Return key facts as bullet points.",
    tools=[google_search],
)
writer = Agent(
    name="writer",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Drafts articles from research.",
    instruction="Write a 300-word article from the research provided. Keep it factual.",
)
pipeline = SequentialAgent(
    name="article_pipeline",
    sub_agents=[researcher, writer],
)
```

The writer automatically receives the researcher's output. No prompt engineering required to pass data along; the framework handles it.

## ParallelAgent: Fan Out, Then Merge

When steps are independent, run them concurrently. A product launch checklist might research competitors, draft the announcement, and check inventory simultaneously. ParallelAgent fans out to all sub-agents at once and collects their results. The speedup is real, and so is the design constraint: parallel steps cannot depend on each other's outputs. If step B needs step A's result, that is a sequence, not a parallel fan-out. Getting this wrong produces race conditions that are maddening to debug, so be strict with yourself about independence.

## LoopAgent: Repeat Until Done

Some processes are iterative by nature: draft, critique, revise, repeat until quality passes a bar. LoopAgent runs its sub-agents in a cycle with a termination condition, usually a maximum iteration count plus a quality check. The classic pattern is a generator agent paired with a critic agent: the generator produces, the critic scores, and the loop exits when the score passes the threshold or iterations run out. Always set the iteration cap. An unbounded loop with an LLM in it is a billing incident waiting to happen, and the critic must have crisp, checkable criteria, not vibes.

## Choosing Between Workflow and Agentic Routing

The rule of thumb: if you can draw the flowchart, use workflow agents. If the next step genuinely depends on interpreting the current situation, let a coordinator agent route dynamically. Most production systems are hybrids: a sequential pipeline where one step is a coordinator that delegates to specialists. Start with the workflow version; add dynamic routing only where the workflow proves too rigid. Determinism is a feature you will miss once it is gone.

lessons.title: Multi-Agent Delegation
lessons.bodyMd:
## One Agent, One Job

The single most reliable scaling pattern in ADK is also the simplest: give each agent one job and let a coordinator delegate. A customer-support system becomes a triage coordinator plus billing, technical, and account specialists. Each specialist has a tight instruction, a small toolset, and a clear description. The coordinator's only job is routing. This beats a monolithic agent because small instructions are easier to write, easier to test, and easier to fix.

## How Delegation Works

In ADK, a coordinator agent lists specialists as sub-agents. When the coordinator decides a task belongs to a specialist, it delegates: the specialist runs with the relevant context, produces a result, and control returns to the coordinator. The coordinator reads each specialist's `description` to make routing decisions, which is why that field matters so much.

```python
from google.adk.agents import Agent

billing = Agent(
    name="billing_specialist",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Handles billing questions: charges, refunds, invoices.",
    instruction="Answer billing questions using lookup_order and refund_policy. Never promise a refund amount; escalate to a human for amounts over $500.",
    tools=[lookup_order, refund_policy],
)
technical = Agent(
    name="technical_specialist",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Handles technical issues: setup, errors, integrations.",
    instruction="Diagnose technical issues using search_knowledge_base. Ask for error messages before speculating.",
    tools=[search_knowledge_base],
)
coordinator = Agent(
    name="support_coordinator",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Routes support requests to the right specialist.",
    instruction=(
        "Classify the request, then delegate to the matching specialist. "
        "If the request spans categories, delegate to each in turn and "
        "synthesize their answers. If no specialist fits, say so honestly."
    ),
    sub_agents=[billing, technical],
)
```

## The Coordinator's Instruction Is the Architecture

Notice how much work the coordinator's instruction does: classify, delegate, synthesize multi-part answers, and admit when nothing fits. That last clause is load-bearing. A coordinator without an honest fallback will force-fit every request into the wrong specialist. Write the fallback first, then the happy paths.

Start every multi-agent design on paper before writing code. Draw the coordinator in the center, list the specialists around it, and write one sentence for each describing exactly what it owns and what it must refuse. If two specialists' sentences overlap, your boundaries are wrong and the coordinator will misroute. Clean boundaries on paper become clean routing in production.

## Testing Delegation

Delegation bugs are routing bugs, and routing bugs are found with adversarial test cases, not happy paths. Build a test list of tricky inputs: a billing question phrased with technical words, a request that spans two specialists, a request that fits none. Run each in a fresh session in the dev UI and check the events pane to confirm the coordinator chose correctly. Every misroute you catch here is a confused customer you never create. Chapter 4's evaluation lesson shows how to automate this so it runs on every change.

lessons.title: MCP and A2A: Connecting to the Wider Ecosystem
lessons.bodyMd:
## Why Protocols Beat Integrations

Every agent framework eventually faces the same problem: there are thousands of tools and data sources, and no framework can build native integrations for all of them. The industry's answer is protocols, shared standards that let any compliant tool work with any compliant framework. ADK supports the two that matter most: MCP and A2A.

## MCP: Model Context Protocol

MCP, originally developed by Anthropic, is now the industry-standard way to expose tools and data sources to agents. An MCP server wraps some capability, a database, a SaaS API, a file system, and presents it in a standard format. An MCP-compatible client, like an ADK agent, can discover and call those capabilities without custom integration code.

In practice, this means your ADK agent can use the growing universe of MCP servers with minimal glue. Need your agent to query Postgres? There is an MCP server for that. Need it to read Google Drive files or hit a ticketing API? MCP servers exist or are easy to write. The pattern is: run the MCP server, point ADK at it, and the server's tools appear in the agent's tool list as if they were native function tools.

```python
from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool import McpToolset

# Tools from an MCP server become ADK tools
db_tools = McpToolset(
    connection_params={
        "command": "npx",
        "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres", "postgresql://localhost/mydb"],
    }
)

root_agent = Agent(
    name="data_assistant",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Answers questions using the company database.",
    instruction="Use the database tools to answer questions. Show your SQL before running it.",
    tools=[db_tools],
)
```

That is the whole integration: a process launch and a tools list entry. When evaluating MCP servers, check who maintains them and what permissions they request; a tool with write access to production deserves the same scrutiny as any deploy.

## A2A: Agent-to-Agent Protocol

If MCP connects agents to tools, A2A connects agents to each other. Google's Agent-to-Agent protocol is an open standard for agents built on different frameworks to discover each other, exchange messages, and collaborate on tasks. Your ADK coordinator can delegate to an agent built with another framework, provided both speak A2A.

For beginners, A2A matters less on day one and more on day one hundred. Early on, your agents all live in ADK and delegate natively. Later, when you acquire a team whose agents run on another stack, or when you want to expose your agent as a service others can call, A2A is the bridge. Design your agent boundaries cleanly now, with crisp descriptions and well-defined inputs, and the protocol migration later is straightforward. Messy agent boundaries are what make cross-framework collaboration painful, not the protocol.

## The Practical Takeaway

Learn MCP now; it immediately multiplies what your agents can do. Understand A2A conceptually; you will reach for it when your agent systems outgrow a single framework. Both are open standards, which means the knowledge transfers even if you later build on a different stack.

lessons.title: Evaluating and Debugging Trajectories
lessons.bodyMd:
## Eyeballing Chats Does Not Scale

The beginner's testing method is chatting with the agent and deciding it "seems fine." This works for exactly one agent and zero regressions. The moment you change an instruction or add a tool, you need to know whether the ten behaviors that worked yesterday still work today. ADK's answer is trajectory evaluation: automated tests that assert on what the agent did, not just what it said.

## What a Trajectory Is

A trajectory is the full record of an agent's execution: the user input, each model reasoning step, each tool call with its arguments, each tool result, and the final response. The dev UI's events pane shows you one trajectory visually. Evaluation turns trajectories into test cases: run the agent on a fixed input, capture the trajectory, and assert properties about it.

## Writing Your First Eval

ADK's eval tooling lets you define test cases as conversation scripts with expected behaviors. A good eval set covers the happy path, the known tricky cases, and the adversarial inputs from your delegation testing. For each case you assert things like: the agent called the right tool, it did not call a forbidden tool, the final answer contains the required information, and it refused or escalated where required.

```bash
adk eval support_coordinator eval_cases.json
```

Start small: five to ten cases covering your most important behaviors. Run them before every instruction change. When a change breaks a case, you have a choice: fix the agent, or update the case because the new behavior is actually better. Both are legitimate; what is not legitimate is changing behavior without noticing.

## The Debugging Loop, Formalized

Evaluation and the dev UI form a complete loop. Evals catch regressions automatically across your whole behavior set. When an eval fails, you reproduce the single case in `adk web`, read the trajectory in the events pane, find the step where reasoning or tool use went wrong, fix the instruction or tool, and rerun the evals. This is the professional version of the "reproduce, inspect, fix" loop from Chapter 2, and it is what separates hobby agents from production agents.

## What to Measure

Track four things over time. Task success rate: did the agent accomplish the goal. Tool precision: did it call the right tools with valid arguments. Escalation correctness: did it ask for help exactly when it should have, neither too often nor too rarely. And cost per task: tokens consumed per completed task, because an agent that succeeds at ten times the necessary cost is a design waiting to be fixed. ADK's eval reports give you the raw material; the discipline of watching the trends is yours.

lessons.title: From Laptop to Production: Deploy Options
lessons.bodyMd:
## The Same Code, New Runtime

The promise that runs through this entire guide is deployment continuity: the agent package you built and tested locally is the artifact you deploy. ADK supports three main targets, and the right choice depends on how much operational control you need.

## Option 1: Agent Runtime (Vertex AI Agent Engine)

Agent Runtime, part of the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, is Google's managed home for ADK agents. You deploy your agent package, and Google handles scaling, session management, and operations. This is the recommended path when you want production without operating infrastructure. Deployment is a CLI command against your Cloud project, and your agent becomes an API endpoint your applications call.

To use it you need a Google Cloud project with billing enabled and Vertex AI API access, which is the moment the free AI Studio key hands off to production credentials. Your agent code does not change; the model backend switches from the AI Studio key to Vertex AI authentication, typically via a service account. Design for this handoff early by keeping credentials in environment configuration, never in code.

## Option 2: Cloud Run

Cloud Run is Google's serverless container platform, and it is the right choice when you want more control over the serving layer or when your agent is one component in a larger service. You containerize your agent with a small web server exposing its API, push the image, and Cloud Run scales it from zero to whatever traffic arrives. You manage the container and the scaling configuration; Google manages the machines.

Choose Cloud Run when you already serve other workloads there and want your agent alongside them, when you need custom networking or VPC access to internal systems, or when your compliance team wants the agent inside your existing container pipeline. The trade-off versus Agent Runtime is operational: more knobs, more responsibility.

## Option 3: Google Kubernetes Engine

GKE is for teams already running Kubernetes who want agents as just another workload in their clusters. You get maximum control over networking, scaling policies, and co-location with other services. You also get maximum operational responsibility. Unless your organization already runs GKE and has opinions about it, prefer one of the first two options; Kubernetes is a powerful answer to a question most agent deployments are not asking.

## The Deployment Command Flow

Regardless of target, the flow has the same shape. First, switch authentication from your AI Studio key to production credentials. Second, run your eval suite one final time against the production configuration; model behavior can shift subtly between backends, and you want proof, not hope. Third, deploy with the ADK tooling for your chosen target. Fourth, smoke-test the deployed endpoint with your core scenarios before sending real traffic. Fifth, wire up logging and monitoring, which the next lesson covers. Deployments are boring on purpose; excitement here means incidents.

lessons.title: Production Checklist and Cost Monitoring
lessons.bodyMd:
## The Pre-Launch Checklist

Run through this list before any agent meets real users. Every item exists because someone skipped it and paid for the lesson.

**Credentials.** No API keys in code, containers, or chat logs. Production uses a service account with the minimum IAM roles the agent needs. The AI Studio key you developed with is deleted or restricted to development use.

**Evals green.** Your trajectory eval suite passes against the production configuration. Not "mostly passes." Green.

**Loop guards.** Every LoopAgent has an iteration cap. Every agent with write tools has explicit instruction about when writing is allowed. There is a global timeout on task execution so a stuck agent fails loudly instead of billing quietly.

**Human escalation paths.** Define exactly when the agent must stop and ask a human: refunds over a threshold, irreversible actions, low-confidence classifications, anything touching production data. Test each escalation path; an untested fallback is a rumor.

**Logging.** Every trajectory is logged with timestamps, tool calls, and model versions. When a user reports a bad outcome, you can replay exactly what happened. ADK's session and event infrastructure gives you this; make sure your deployment preserves it.

**Rollback plan.** Know how to revert to the previous agent version in minutes. Version your agent packages, keep the last known-good deployment, and practice the rollback once before you need it.

## Cost Monitoring

Agent costs are token costs plus compute, and both scale with usage patterns you must watch. Set up billing alerts on your Cloud project from day one; the first alert should fire long before the bill surprises you. Track cost per completed task, not just total spend, because total spend grows with success while cost per task reveals efficiency regressions.

The biggest cost lever is model selection per step. Audit which agents actually need Pro-class reasoning and demote the rest to Flash. The second lever is loop discipline: capped iterations, early exits, and critics with crisp pass criteria. The third is context hygiene: inject only the state each step needs instead of the entire session history. A production agent that costs three cents per task instead of thirty is not a minor optimization; at scale it is the difference between a viable product and a write-off.

## The Ongoing Practice

Deployment is not the finish line; it is the start of operations. Review failed trajectories weekly and turn each one into either an instruction fix or a new eval case. Watch your escalation rate: rising escalations mean the world changed or your agent degraded. Keep a changelog of instruction and tool changes alongside your eval results so you can correlate behavior changes with their causes. Agents are software, and software needs the same operational discipline as any service you have ever run. The teams that treat agents as living systems win; the teams that deploy and forget get paged.
